content: 1. The study by Bloss (2004) was excluded because it did not investigate the effects of continued breastfeeding beyond 12 months. It focused on the introduction of complementary foods before 6 months as a risk factor. 2. Bobrow (2013) was excluded because it did not specifically study continued breastfeeding as defined. The breastfeeding durations analyzed were less than 6 months, 6-9 months, and more than 10 months. 3. Boucher (2017) was excluded because it did not compare continued breastfeeding with shorter durations of breastfeeding. Instead, it analyzed the effects of breastfeeding duration on child development, ADHD, and autism using regression analyses. 4. Bravo (1997) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It compared exclusive breastfeeding for less than 4 months with more than 4 months. 5. Briend (1989) was excluded due to the absence of a control group. It compared breastfed versus non-breastfed children aged 12-35 months but did not provide details on the breastfeeding duration of weaned children. 6. Brinton (1995) was excluded because it was a case-control study with cases selected from hospital admissions and registries, which were not representative of the population. 7. Brion (2011) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It compared breastfeeding durations of less than 1 month, 1-3 months, 3-5 months, and 6 months or more. 8. Brun (1995) was excluded because it did not present data in case and control groups to meet inclusion criteria. The lactation durations analyzed were 1-9 months, 10-19 months, and more than 20 months. 9. Bulbul (2008) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Feeding habits were analyzed for each month in the first six months, including exclusive breastfeeding, breastfeeding with formula, breastfeeding with cow’s milk, breastfeeding with additional food, formula only, and additional food without breastfeeding. 10. Buyken (2008) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It analyzed breastfeeding durations of more than 4 months, using the lower limit of German recommendations for complementary food introduction. 11. Byrne (2018) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. 12. Camayo (2008) was excluded because it was a case-control study conducted in a hospital setting, which was not representative of the population. 13. Cando (2019) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It analyzed the effects of exclusive breastfeeding for durations less than and more than 6 months. 14. Caulfield (1996) was excluded because it did not compare continued breastfeeding with shorter durations. Data on breastfeeding at various ages were collected as either still breastfeeding or not breastfeeding at the time of the survey. 15. Chaiffarino (2005) was excluded because it was a hospital-based case-control study. 16. Chang-Claude (2000) was excluded because it was a case-control study with cases identified from hospitals. 17. Chantry (2004) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It compared lactation with no lactation. 18. Chantry (2007) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It compared anemia and iron status (serum ferritin) across five groups: formula-fed only, full breastfeeding for 1 month, 1-3 months, 4-5 months, and 6 months. 19. Chiu (2011) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It analyzed breastfeeding durations of 6 months and 9 months. 20. Chowdhury (2002) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It analyzed cumulative lactation durations of 0-60 months, 60-120 months, and more than 120 months. 21. Clark (2006) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into three groups: less than 2 months, 2-8 months, and more than 8 months. 22. Coogan (1999) was excluded because it was a hospital-based case-control study. 23. Cooke-Hubley (2019) was excluded because data on continued breastfeeding were not available. It provided data on breastfeeding durations of less than 1 month, 1-6 months, and more than 6 months, with multivariate regression performed using lactation duration as a covariate. 24. Cruz (2017) was excluded because it was a case-control study not representative of the entire population. 25. Cumming (1993) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It analyzed breastfeeding durations of less than 3 months, 3-6 months, 6-9 months, and more than 9 months. 26. Dahlquist (1991) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding durations of less than 3 months were analyzed as a risk factor for diabetes in regression analyses. 27. Daniels (2002) was excluded because it was a hospital-based case-control study. 28. Darmawikarta (2016) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. 29. Darsene (2017) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It analyzed the effects of breastfeeding for more than 2 years versus less than 2 years on undernutrition. 30. Dasanayake (2002) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. No data on discrete groups with different breastfeeding durations were reported. 31. Davisse-Paturet (2020) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It analyzed breastfeeding durations of less than 1 month, 1-4 months, and more than 4 months. 32. Delgado (2017) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding duration was categorized as less than 24 months, 24-35 months, and 36 months. 33. de Matos (2011) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It analyzed breastfeeding durations of less than 2 months and more than 2 months. 34. Den Dekker (2016) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into four groups: less than 2 months, 2-4 months, 4-6 months, and more than 6 months. 35. De Silva (2010) was excluded because it was a hospital-based case-control study. 36. Dewey (1991) was excluded because it lacked a control group. It studied the growth patterns of infants breastfed for at least 12 months. 37. Dewey (1993) was excluded because the control group consisted of formula-fed babies. 38. Dieu (2007) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It analyzed breastfeeding duration as a continuous variable using regression analyses. 39. Dini (2000) was excluded because data on continued breastfeeding were not available. It compared the effects of breastfeeding for less than 2 years, more than 2 years, and no breastfeeding on dental caries. 40. Donkor (2017) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It analyzed the effects of exclusive breastfeeding for less and more than 4 months on obesity. 41. Durmus (2012) was excluded because it studied breastfeeding durations of less than and more than 4 months. 42. Egan (1998) was excluded because it was a case-control study with subjects having a family history of cancer. 43. Ehlayel (2008) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Prolonged breastfeeding was defined as more than 6 months. 44. Elliot (1997) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It analyzed exclusive breastfeeding for more and less than 2 months. 45. Elliott (2008) was excluded because it did not study controlled breastfeeding. 46. Elwood (2005) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding durations of less than and greater than 3 months were analyzed. 47. Enger (1997) was excluded because it was a case-control study with cases selected from a cancer surveillance registry, not representative of the population. 48. Enger (1998) was excluded because it was a hospital-based case-control study. 49. Eriksson (2003) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It reported breastfeeding durations of up to 8 months. 50. Fancony (2020) was excluded because continued breastfeeding was defined as children over 5 months who were both breastfed and complementary fed. Data were analyzed for the risk of iron deficiency anemia using regression analyses. 51. Farajzadeh (2011) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding duration was analyzed as a continuous variable. 52. Fatemi (2019) was excluded because it compared formula-only feeding or breastfeeding for less than 18 months with breastfeeding for 18-24 months. 53. Fawzi (1998) was excluded because it did not compare prolonged and shorter breastfeeding durations. 54. Feldens (2010) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding data were collected at 6 months and 1 year but not beyond. 55. Fikadu (2014) was excluded because it lacked a control group. 56. Flohr (2011) was excluded because data on continued breastfeeding were not presented. Breastfeeding was categorized as never breastfed, breastfed for less than 6 months, or breastfed for more than 6 months. 57. Folayan (2010) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding duration was analyzed as a continuous variable. 58. Foroushani (2010) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding duration was analyzed as a continuous variable. 59. Fox (1993) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Lactation duration was used as a continuous variable in regression analyses. 60. Fox (2013) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding duration was analyzed as a continuous variable, and regression analysis was performed to study its impact on Alzheimer’s disease. 61. Francisco (1993) was excluded because it did not use lactation duration at all. It compared mortality risk in breastfed, partially weaned with some vitamin A, partially weaned without vitamin A, and fully weaned groups. 62. Frank (2019) was excluded because the subjects were positive for high-risk genes for Type 1 diabetes, making them unrepresentative of the healthy population. 63. Freudenheim (1997) was excluded because it was a case-control study with cases identified from two hospitals, not representative of the population. 64. Furberg (1999) was excluded because it was a case-control study. 65. Gale (2004) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. 66. Gammon (2002) was excluded because it was an institution-based case-control study. 67. Garden (2012) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Children were classified into three groups based on breastfeeding duration: less than 3 months, 3-6 months, and more than 6 months. 68. Gewa (2012) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding duration was analyzed as a continuous variable using regression analyses. 69. Ghiasvand (2011) was excluded because it was a hospital-based case-control study. 70. Giamba de Lima (2001) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It analyzed risk factors for breast cancer in a cohort. 71. Girma (2019) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It provided the risk for underweight in children breastfed for less than 24 months versus more than 24 months. 72. Goldfield (2006) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It compared breastfed versus non-breastfed children. 73. Gomez-Sanchiz (2003) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Infants were classified based on the type of feeding received: formula-fed since birth, breastfed (exclusive or partial) for up to 4 months, and breastfed (exclusive or partial) for longer than 4 months. 74. Gomez-Sanchiz (2004) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Infants were classified into the same feeding categories as in the previous study. 75. Gopalan (1992) was excluded because it was a review of breastfeeding’s impact on maternal and child health. 76. Gopinath (2012) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding duration was categorized as never breastfed, less than 1 month, 1-3 months, 3-6 months, and more than 6 months. 77. Greggi (2000) was excluded because it was a hospital-based case-control study. 78. Grimshaw (2013) was excluded because it was a case-control study not representative of the entire population. 79. Grjibovski (2008) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Four categories of breastfeeding duration were used: less than 2 months, 2-3 months, 4-5 months, and 6 months or more. 80. Gunderson (2014) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It compared breastfeeding durations of more than 9 months with shorter durations. 81. Gunderson (2014a) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Women were categorized into four lactation groups based on cumulative duration for all post-baseline births: less than 1 month, 1-6 months, 6-10 months, and more than 10 months. 82. Gunderson (2015) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. The overall lactation duration was divided into four categories to evenly distribute the analytic sample and represent clinically relevant periods of lactation. 83. Gunther (2013) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Infants not fully breastfed for up to 2 weeks were classified as “never fully breastfed.” 84. Guven (2005) was excluded because the subjects were not healthy. All enrolled subjects had Type 1 diabetes. 85. Hallonsten (1995) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Children were divided into four groups based on caries status and breastfeeding. 86. Han (2004) was excluded because it was a case-control study. Cases were from hospitals in Wuhan, China, and controls were patients treated for non-malignant conditions. 87. Han (2012) was excluded because it was a case-only analysis. All subjects had rhinitis. 88. Han (2019) was excluded because all subjects had rhinitis, making it not representative of a population cohort. 89. Harding (2007) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding durations analyzed were less than 1 month, 1-6 months, and more than 6 months. 90. Hassa (2005) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. 91. Hay (2008) was excluded because it did not compare continued breastfeeding with shorter durations. It compared children breastfed versus not breastfed at 24 months of age. 92. Hayosh (2015) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Three groups of lactation duration were studied: no breastfeeding, breastfeeding for 0-6 months, and breastfeeding for more than 9 months. 93. Heard-Lipsmeyer (2020) was excluded because data on continued breastfeeding were not available separately. Breastfeeding duration was analyzed as a continuous variable using multivariate regression analyses. 94. Hediger (2001) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding was categorized into durations of 2 months or less, 3-5 months, 6-8 months, and 9 months or more. 95. Hewat (1986) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. It analyzed women’s perceptions of their breastfeeding experiences. 96. Hosaka (2013) was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Study participants and children were divided into two groups based on the median duration of breastfeeding.
